A2.text:
Julian is a young lawyer in Baku. His friend Yunus is a potter. Yunus has a small workshop in Icherisheher. He makes beautiful handmade bowls and plates.

Julian works on a computer all day. One Saturday, he visited Yunus. “I want to learn your craft,” he said. “Can I be your apprentice?”

Yunus laughed. “You need a lot of patience,” he said. “But you can try. First, learn the ropes.”

Every Saturday, Julian went to the workshop. It was not easy. His first bowls were terrible. They fell down on the wheel or broke in the oven.

“Why is this so hard?” Julian asked. “In the shops, there are thousands of bowls.”

“Those are mass-produced,” Yunus said. “A machine makes them. My bowls are a labour of love. And they are made to last.”

After two months, Julian made a small blue bowl. He painted a simple pattern on it. The bowl was a little crooked. It was imperfect, but Julian was proud.

He gave it to his mother for her birthday. “It is not perfect,” he said.

His mother held it in her hands. “It is perfect for me,” she said.

Now she uses the crooked bowl every day for her sugar. When guests come, she always says, “My son made this.”

B1.text:
Julian spent his weekdays in a glass office tower, reading contracts until his eyes hurt. His oldest friend Yunus spent his in a small, dusty workshop in Icherisheher, turning wet clay into bowls, jugs and plates.

One Saturday, he surprised them both. “Teach me,” he said. “I want to learn your craft. I'll be your apprentice — unpaid, of course.”

Yunus wiped his hands on his apron and looked at him for a long time. “It takes patience,” he said. “More than your law school ever did. But fine. Come every Saturday at nine, and first you learn the ropes: clay, water, the wheel, the kiln.”

The first month was humiliating. Julian's clay flew off the wheel, collapsed into shapeless piles or cracked in the kiln. Once, a half-finished jug spun off and hit Yunus's cat.

“I don't understand,” Julian complained, covered in grey dust. “You can buy a hundred bowls for the price of a dinner. Why does anyone do this?”

“Those bowls are mass-produced,” Yunus said, gently shaping the rim of a vase. “A machine makes ten thousand, all the same, and in two years they're chipped and in the bin. Each of mine is a labour of love. And they're made to last — my grandfather's plates are still on my mother's table.”

By the end of the second month, Julian finally finished something: a small bowl, glazed in deep blue, with a simple wave pattern around the edge. It leaned slightly to one side. Imperfect, Yunus said, but alive.

Julian gave it to his mother on her sixtieth birthday, apologising before she had even opened the paper. “It's crooked. I know. It's not like the handmade ones in the shops.”

His mother turned it in her hands and said nothing for a moment. Then she put it in the centre of the table.

It holds her sugar now, every day. And whenever guests visit, she makes sure to mention, casually, that her son — the lawyer — made it himself.

B2.text:
Julian spent his weekdays on the twentieth floor of a glass tower, reading contracts until the clauses blurred together. His oldest friend Yunus spent his in a cramped, dusty workshop in Icherisheher, coaxing wet clay into bowls, jugs and plates. Whenever Julian dropped by, he noticed that something inside him unclenched as he watched Yunus work.

One Saturday, he surprised them both. “Teach me,” he said. “I want to learn the craft properly. Take me on as your apprentice — unpaid, naturally.”

Yunus wiped his hands on his apron and regarded him for a long moment. “It demands patience,” he said. “More than any law exam. But all right. Saturdays, nine o'clock. First you learn the ropes: the clay, the water, the wheel, the kiln. Then we'll see.”

The first month was a sustained humiliation. Julian's clay flew off the wheel, slumped into shapeless heaps or cracked in the kiln. On one memorable occasion, a half-formed jug spun loose and struck Yunus's cat, who has refused to set foot in the workshop on Saturdays ever since.

“I don't get it,” Julian protested, coated in grey dust to the elbows. “You can buy a hundred bowls for the price of a dinner. Why does anybody bother?”

“Because those are mass-produced,” Yunus replied, delicately thinning the rim of a vase. “A machine stamps out ten thousand identical copies, and in two years they're chipped and thrown away. Every piece I make is a labour of love — and made to last. My grandfather's plates are still on my mother's table.”

By the end of the second month, Julian finally produced something that survived: a small bowl in deep cobalt glaze, ringed with a simple wave pattern. It leaned unmistakably to one side. Imperfect, Yunus pronounced, but undeniably alive.

Julian gave it to his mother on her sixtieth birthday, apologising before she had even unwrapped it. “It's crooked, I know. Nothing like the handmade pieces in the galleries.”

She turned it slowly in her hands and was silent for a while. Then she placed it at the centre of the table.

It has held her sugar every day since. And whenever guests visit, she contrives to mention, as if in passing, that her son — the lawyer, you understand — made it with his own hands.
